source.heading: All walks of life
source.body:
Nothing here describes any one person. Every number below is from a survey, with a range around it.

**The overall picture.** Compass's African American profile for 2020 to 2024 shows a median household income of $48,200, give or take $2,398. In the same profile, 36.2 percent of households earn under $35,000 and 22.2 percent earn $100,000 or more. Both ends are large, and more than one household in five is at the higher end. Owner-occupied homes are 30.1 percent. Of adults 25 and older, 89.5 percent finished high school and 21.9 percent hold a bachelor's degree or more. Among working-age adults, 67.3 percent are employed. Below poverty: 21.4 percent ([Minnesota Compass](https://www.mncompass.org/topics/demographics/cultural-communities/african-american)).

**Wealth.** No Minnesota count of Black millionaires or study of wealthy Black families was found. What exists points to a deep gap in household wealth, measured for all Black Minnesotans together. The 2024 Status of Women and Girls in Minnesota report, as filed with the Minnesota House, says the median net worth of Black households in Minnesota is $0, against $211,000 for white households and $18,000 for Latino households, and calls Minnesota's racial wealth gap the third largest in the country; the passage does not state the year of its data ([Status of Women & Girls in Minnesota 2024, via Minnesota House](https://www.house.mn.gov/comm/docs/mHvOsaQu6UeTXRNz7uVaow.pdf)). The Minnesota Budget Project, drawing on Prosperity Now's 2020 scorecard and 2016 data, said wealth figures were then available only for white Minnesotans, and that almost three-quarters of Black households lacked enough savings to cover three months of basic needs ([Minnesota Budget Project](https://mnbudgetproject.org/blog/racial-opportunity-gaps-persist-despite-prosperity-for-some)). These are statewide medians. They do not describe any one family, and they sit beside the fifth of households earning $100,000 or more.

**Prominent names.** Public careers show the range. Alan Page, the first Black judge on the Minnesota Supreme Court ([MNopedia](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/african-americans-minnesota)). Dave Winfield, raised in Rondo, Baseball Hall of Famer, whose family foundation's Winfield Awards have run since 1977 ([Spokesman-Recorder, June 1, 2026](https://spokesman-recorder.com/2026/06/01/david-winfield-statue-st-paul/)). Tracey Williams-Dillard, third-generation owner of the state's oldest Black-owned business ([WCCO](https://www.cbsnews.com/amp/minnesota/news/minnesota-spokesman-recorder-90th-anniversary)). The Minnesota Black Chamber of Commerce's first Black Business Hall of Fame class in August 2026 named her with Sharon Smith-Akinsanya, Gloria Freeman, Lea Harget, Frederick Blockton, Frank Brown, Frederic Estes, Ezell Jones and Prince Wallace, with Candice Ellis and Richard Copeland honored after their deaths ([Spokesman-Recorder, Aug. 13, 2026](https://spokesman-recorder.com/2026/08/13/minnesota-black-business-hall-of-fame-inaugural-class/)).

**Professionals and the middle class.** Rondo had professionals and builders among its families. Marvin Anderson, a retired lawyer and longtime State Law Librarian, grew up there, and his father and partners built the Rangh Court townhomes in 1947 ([AARP](https://www.aarp.org/livable-communities/getting-around/info-2023/before-the-highway-rondo-saint-paul-minnesota-marvin-anderson.html)). Natalie Hudson served as Chief Justice from October 2023 until her retirement on Sept. 30, 2026 ([FOX 9, 2026](https://www.fox9.com/news/minnesota-supreme-court-chief-justice-natalie-hudson-retire-september)). Her father was Macalester College's first Black football coach ([WCCO, Aug. 23, 2023](https://www.cbsnews.com/amp/minnesota/news/natalie-hudson-is-named-the-first-black-chief-justice-of-minnesota-supreme-court)). Damon Jenkins leads Minnesota for First Independence Bank ([Spokesman-Recorder, June 29, 2026](https://spokesman-recorder.com/2026/06/29/first-independence-bank-st-paul-university-avenue/)). Architect James Garrett Jr., who describes himself as a fifth-generation St. Paulite from the Rondo community, founded the firm 4RM+ULA in 2002; in 2020 he noted that 0.6 percent of Minnesota architects are Black ([Mpls.St.Paul Magazine, Nov. 10, 2020](https://mspmag.com/home-and-design/change-maker/)). The Minnesota Association of Black Lawyers, founded in September 1995, says its members have served on the Minnesota Supreme Court, as chief judges, prosecutors and U.S. Attorney, and in private practice ([MABL](https://www.mabl.org/legacy)).

**Occupations.** Among employed Minnesotans who list Black as their only race (183,871 people, 2020 to 2024, including immigrants), 32.3 percent work in management, business, science and arts jobs, against 45.5 percent of all employed Minnesotans. Women hold slightly more of these professional jobs than men (30,634 to 28,847) ([Census Reporter, table C24010B](https://api.censusreporter.org/1.0/data/show/acs2024_5yr?table_ids=C24010B&geo_ids=04000US27); [all Minnesotans, table C24010](https://api.censusreporter.org/1.0/data/show/acs2024_5yr?table_ids=C24010&geo_ids=04000US27)).

**Working families.** Compass shows working-age women employed at 70.0 percent and men at 64.7 percent. Among households, 9.0 percent are married couples with children, 11.6 percent married couples without children, 13.6 percent single mothers, 1.4 percent single fathers and 40.8 percent people living alone ([Minnesota Compass](https://www.mncompass.org/topics/demographics/cultural-communities/african-american)).

**Hardship.** More than half of households (52.2 percent) spend too much of their income on housing, including 62.6 percent of renters ([Minnesota Compass](https://www.mncompass.org/topics/demographics/cultural-communities/african-american)). A May 2026 discussion put median income at about $39,000 in North Minneapolis and about $89,000 citywide, as a speaker's figures rather than a checked table ([Insight News via The Hub, May 22, 2026](https://thehub.news/fraud-scrutiny-tests-trusted-black-institutions/?amp=1)). The state council for Minnesotans of African Heritage, in a 2025 advocacy handout covering all Black Minnesotans, says more than 70 percent of Minnesota households own homes and less than 30 percent of Black Minnesotans do, with majority-Black neighborhoods undervalued by about $48,000 per home ([CMAH handout, March 2025](https://www.lrl.mn.gov/archive/minutes/senate/2025/jobs/20250324/Jobs_20250324_SF2423-CMAH-Black-Homeownership-Factsheet-handout.pdf)). The Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis, as reported by WCCO, found a 29 percent Black homeownership rate in the Twin Cities in 2024 and a Black-white gap of 46.9, the widest among comparable metros ([WCCO, May 10, 2026](https://www.cbsnews.com/minnesota/news/black-homeownership-twin-cities-gap-minneapolis-federal-reserve/)).

**Compared with African-born neighbors.** The same Compass tables show why the combined "Black" figures can mislead. Median household income: African American $48,200, Somali $49,554 (give or take $6,519), Nigerian $76,000 (give or take $22,344). Owner-occupied homes: African American 30.1 percent, Somali 15.6 percent, Nigerian 45.0 percent. Bachelor's degree or more: African American 21.9 percent, Nigerian 55.3 percent ([African American](https://www.mncompass.org/topics/demographics/cultural-communities/african-american); [Somali](https://www.mncompass.org/topics/demographics/cultural-communities/somali); [Nigerian](https://www.mncompass.org/topics/demographics/cultural-communities/nigerian)). The margins are wide for the smaller groups. A difference like this describes a pattern across households, not any family, and these tables do not explain its causes.

source.heading: Health and wellbeing, broadly
source.body:
**A U.S.-born Black focus.** The Minnesota Department of Human Services produced a report centered on U.S.-born Black Minnesotans, "Building Racial Equity into the Walls of Minnesota Medicaid." Its author wrote in 2022 that about 41.5 percent of Black Minnesotans and about 64 percent of Black children rely on Medicaid, and that among enrollees of the same average age, asthma, heart failure and depression were about three times higher for U.S.-born Black enrollees than for those born abroad ([Spokesman-Recorder, Feb. 18, 2022](https://spokesman-recorder.com/2022/02/18/report-aims-to-close-gap-in-health-disparities-for-u-s-born-blacks-minnesotans/)). The article does not explain why, and that remains an open question.

**Maternal and infant health.** The state's 2017 to 2021 report gives 40.3 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births for Black parents, 2.3 times the statewide 17.9 ([Minnesota Department of Health, Jan. 12, 2026](https://www.health.state.mn.us/news/pressrel/2026/maternal011226.html)). Hennepin County reports that in 2019 only 64 percent of U.S.-born Black pregnant people received appropriate care during pregnancy ([Hennepin County](https://www.hennepincounty.gov/government/projects-initiatives/health/maternal-health-initiative)).

**Community-rooted care.** NorthPoint Health and Wellness has served North Minneapolis since 1968, at 2220 Plymouth Avenue North, with medical, dental, behavioral and eye care and human services ([NorthPoint](https://www.northpointhealth.org/)). Roots Community Birth Center, founded by Rebecca Polston, was described in 2016 as the only African American-owned birth center in the state ([Minnesota Daily, Oct. 31, 2016](https://mndaily.com/210611/city/stbirth)) and still practices at 1901 44th Avenue North ([Roots](https://www.rootsbirthcenter.com/)). The Cultural Wellness Center, founded in 1996 with Elder Atum Azzahir as founder and director, offers doula training, rites of passage and a Community Health Hub Kitchen ([Cultural Wellness Center](https://www.culturalwellnesscenter.org/); [Spokesman-Recorder](https://spokesman-recorder.com/2026/10/16/dreamland-on-38th-groundbreaking/)). Sabathani's programs cover maternal health, a Healing Circle for Black Mothers, smoking cessation and more ([Sabathani](https://www.sabathani.org/)).

**Coverage.** In the Compass profile, 5.6 percent lack health insurance ([Minnesota Compass](https://www.mncompass.org/topics/demographics/cultural-communities/african-american)).

findings: Do not broaden the Compass African American profile denominator to all Black Minnesotans; candidate does that. Retain named populations and dated health measures.

source.heading: Businesses and commercial life
source.body:
A separate list gives each business with its current status. It names Black-owned businesses without always being able to separate U.S.-born from African-born or Caribbean owners, and the sources do not always say. What stands out:

**Business districts.** West Broadway and Plymouth Avenue in North Minneapolis; 38th Street and Fourth Avenue on the Southside; Selby Avenue and University Avenue in St. Paul's Rondo and Frogtown. The West Broadway Business and Area Coalition, led by Kristall Porter, talks publicly about displacement, insurance costs and commercial financing ([BuyBlack.org, May 27, 2026](https://www.buyblack.org/articles/west-broadway-s-future-empowering-north-minneapolis-black-community)). The Capri Theater dates to 1927 (same source).

**A list made by the community's own paper.** The Spokesman-Recorder and Sister Spokesman named 50 finalists for 2026, by nomination count, in food, hair and nails, wellness, retail and professional services, confirming each as Black-owned with a website and physical location. Winners are to be announced Nov. 7, 2026 ([Spokesman-Recorder, July 17, 2026](https://spokesman-recorder.com/2026/07/17/best-of-black-business-2026-finalists/)). Many finalists' own pages show them operating in 2026. Camden Social, Alfonso and Kathryn Mayfield's restaurant at 4601 Lyndale Avenue North, takes reservations ([Camden Social](https://thecamdensocial.com/); [KSTP](https://kstp.com/kstp-news/top-news/camden-social-aiming-for-change-in-north-minneapolis/)). Black Garnet Books on University Avenue hosted a University of Minnesota Black History Month event on Feb. 3, 2026 ([University of Minnesota](https://diversity.umn.edu/news-events/black-history-month-events-university-minnesota)). Strive, a downtown Minneapolis bookstore and publisher founded by Mary Taris in 2018, posts weekday hours ([Strive](https://strivepubandco.com/)), and Lutunji's Palate, a bakery-cafe and social enterprise in Elliot Park, books holiday parties ([Lutunji's Palate](https://www.lutunjispalate.com/)). Kente Circle offers family and couples therapy on East 38th Street ([Kente Circle](https://www.kentecircle.com/)), and The Curl District is a natural hair salon in St. Paul ([The Curl District](https://thecurldistrict.com/)).

**Banking.** First Independence Bank, Black-owned and founded in Detroit in 1970, became the first Black-owned full-service bank in the Twin Cities in 2022. It opened at 627 University Avenue West on June 24, 2026, and keeps a branch at 2217 East Lake Street ([Spokesman-Recorder, June 29, 2026](https://spokesman-recorder.com/2026/06/29/first-independence-bank-st-paul-university-avenue/)).

**What has closed.** Breaking Bread Cafe, still found on many lists of Black-owned places, is marked closed by its parent nonprofit, Appetite for Change ([Appetite for Change](https://www.afcmn.org/breaking-bread)). Readers should check any older list before relying on it.

**What is being built.** Dreamland on 38th, an $8 million Black-led building at 3800 Third Avenue South, broke ground Oct. 10, 2026, and is planned to finish in 2027 ([Spokesman-Recorder, Oct. 16, 2026](https://spokesman-recorder.com/2026/10/16/dreamland-on-38th-groundbreaking/)). Its name echoes Dreamland Café, which opened nearby in 1939 ([MNopedia, Southside](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/place/southside-african-american-community-minneapolis)). In Brooklyn Center, a Black Business Village plan on eight acres has a preliminary agreement but no guarantee of construction ([Hoodline, July 20, 2026](https://hoodline.com/2026/07/brooklyn-center-s-8-acre-lot-poised-to-become-black-business-village-hub/)).

**Support groups and events.** The Minnesota Black Chamber of Commerce, led since early 2026 by Yolanda Pierson, held its gala on Aug. 8, 2026 ([Spokesman-Recorder, Aug. 13, 2026](https://spokesman-recorder.com/2026/08/13/minnesota-black-business-hall-of-fame-inaugural-class/)). Minneapolis ran its sixth Black Business Week from July 27 to Aug. 2, 2026 ([City of Minneapolis](https://www.minneapolismn.gov/things-to-do/events/2026-events/july/black-business-week/)), with events run by ROHO Collective, the Northside Economic Opportunity Network and others ([Spokesman-Recorder, July 23, 2026](https://spokesman-recorder.com/2026/07/23/minneapolis-black-business-week-2026-guide/)). 

**Professional firms.** Published lists of Black-owned law, accounting and insurance firms are scarce, and that is a gap in the sources, not proof the firms are absent. Firms with public evidence include H&S Bookkeeping, a Spokesman-Recorder 2026 finalist with an office at 3300 Bass Lake Road in Brooklyn Center ([H&S Bookkeeping](https://hsbookkeeping.com/)); BLK Mortgage Company in Brooklyn Park, also a finalist ([Spokesman-Recorder, July 17, 2026](https://spokesman-recorder.com/2026/07/17/best-of-black-business-2026-finalists/)); and 4RM+ULA, James Garrett Jr.'s architecture firm, which designed the Juxtaposition Arts campus and the Rondo Commemorative Plaza and is listed by AIA Minnesota at 370 Wabasha Street in St. Paul ([AIA Minnesota](https://www.aia-mn.org/firm/4rmula/); [Mpls.St.Paul Magazine, 2020](https://mspmag.com/home-and-design/change-maker/)). For lawyers, the Minnesota Association of Black Lawyers offers attorney referrals and says some members make up "the largest minority-controlled law firm in the Midwest," without naming it ([MABL](https://www.mabl.org/legacy); [MABL home](https://www.mabl.org/)). Its board for 2025 to 2026 is led by Jeremiah Allison, associate counsel for the Minnesota Vikings ([MABL board](https://www.mabl.org/team)).

**Media.** Beside the Spokesman-Recorder and Insight News, BLCK Press describes its mission as reconnecting news to Black culture, won a regional Emmy in 2024 and was publishing current stories in 2026 ([BLCK Press](https://www.blckpress.com/who-we-are); [BLCK Press home](https://www.blckpress.com/)).

source.heading: Religion and spiritual life
source.body:
**The Black church, from freedom seekers onward.** Pilgrim Baptist in St. Paul began in 1863 with people who escaped slavery in Missouri, led by Robert Hickman, and was formally established in 1866. It moved to Rondo in 1928 and stands on Central Avenue today, with Rev. Dr. Charles Gill as senior pastor. Members helped found the local Urban League and NAACP chapters and Hallie Q. Brown ([Spokesman-Recorder, Feb. 22, 2026](https://spokesman-recorder.com/2026/02/22/pilgrim-baptist-church-minnesota-history/); [MPR News, June 23, 2023](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2023/06/23/160-years-of-sanctuary-at-pilgrim-baptist-church)).

**Other congregations.** The Minnesota Historical Society's guide names St. James A.M.E., organized in 1863; St. Peter's A.M.E.; Bethesda Baptist, the oldest Black Baptist congregation in Minneapolis; Zion Baptist; Fellowship Missionary Baptist; Mount Olivet Baptist in Frogtown; and St. Philip's Episcopal ([MNHS library guide](https://libguides.mnhs.org/aafh/church)). Sabathani Baptist formed in 1962 at 3802 Third Avenue South ([MNopedia, Southside](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/place/southside-african-american-community-minneapolis)). Greater Friendship Missionary Baptist hosted a health care rally on Oct. 21, 2026, with a preliminary survey by the Black Church Power Project ([Spokesman-Recorder, Oct. 26, 2026](https://spokesman-recorder.com/2026/10/26/black-minnesotans-health-care-rally-faith-in-minnesotav/)). Pilgrim Baptist posts its Sunday schedule at 732 Central Avenue West ([Pilgrim Baptist](https://pilgrimbaptistchurch.org/)), and Mount Olivet Baptist, whose history pages begin in 1922, posts a Sunday 10:30 a.m. service with a livestream ([Mount Olivet](https://www.mtolivetbaptistchurch.org/)). Greater Friendship Missionary Baptist educators founded Friendship Academy of the Arts in 2000 (see section 10). This is a partial list, and current services were not confirmed for every congregation named.

**How faith shaped place.** The City of Minneapolis notes that Black congregations often did not own their buildings and so had to move when landlords changed plans; some were lost to fire. When Jewish families left North Minneapolis around the 1950s, some Black churches moved into former synagogues, such as First Church of God in Christ ([City of Minneapolis, Aug. 19, 2025](https://www.minneapolismn.gov/media/-www-content-assets/documents/Religion-Houses-of-Worship.pdf)).

**African American Muslims.** The city's summary dates some African American conversion to Islam to the early 1900s (same source). Masjid An-Nur, at Lyndale and 18th Avenue North, grew from Nation of Islam teachings and moved toward Sunni Islam under Warith Deen Mohammed. A 2021 profile described more than 300 worshippers, a majority-African American congregation with growing Somali, Egyptian, Oromo, Bangladeshi and Turkish membership, and an Al-Maa'uun program reaching 300 to 400 families ([Mpls.St.Paul Magazine, Nov. 1, 2021](https://mspmag.com/arts-and-culture/imam-makram-el-amin-community-public-safety/)). Here African American and African-born Muslims worship under one roof. Its Al-Maa'uun program invited North Minneapolis residents to a meeting at the masjid on April 1, 2026, to help shape the future North Minneapolis Resilience Hub site ([Masjid An Nur](https://www.masjidannur.org/)).

**Other paths.** The Cultural Wellness Center teaches ancient wisdom, genealogy and rites of passage for people of African descent ([Cultural Wellness Center](https://www.culturalwellnesscenter.org/)). No Minnesota data was found on how many Black Minnesotans belong to each tradition or to none. As national background only: Pew Research Center's 2021 survey of more than 8,600 Black adults found 66 percent Protestant, 6 percent Catholic, 3 percent other Christian, 3 percent other faiths (Islam the most common) and 21 percent unaffiliated, with about 3 in 10 Black Gen Z and Millennial adults unaffiliated compared with 11 percent of Baby Boomers ([Pew Research Center, Feb. 16, 2021](https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2021/02/16/faith-among-black-americans/)). Whether Minnesota follows that pattern is not known from these sources.

source.heading: Arts, media, sports and culture
source.body:
**Press and radio.** The Spokesman and the Recorder first appeared Aug. 10, 1934 ([Spokesman-Recorder, Aug. 4, 2026](https://spokesman-recorder.com/2026/08/04/msr-92nd-anniversary-cecil-newman-legacy-2/)). Newman's granddaughter Tracey Williams-Dillard is CEO and publisher, and the family says it has never missed a publication day. The paper's own account and a magazine profile date the merger of the two titles and her leadership to 2000 ([Mpls.St.Paul Magazine, Feb. 19, 2024](https://mspmag.com/arts-and-culture/tracey-williams-dillard-on-the-living-legacy-of-the-minnesot)). In 2026 she said corporate leaders and wealthy people are not investing in the Black press ([Spokesman-Recorder](https://spokesman-recorder.com/2026/08/04/msr-92nd-anniversary-cecil-newman-legacy-2/)). The city's Heritage Preservation Commission voted 8-0 on Oct. 6, 2026, to recommend the building at 3744 Fourth Avenue South for the National Register, with the state review board considering it Nov. 10 ([Spokesman-Recorder, Oct. 16, 2026](https://spokesman-recorder.com/2026/10/16/msr-headquarters-national-register-historic-places/)). Gordon Parks got his start as a staff photographer there, the paper says ([Spokesman-Recorder](https://spokesman-recorder.com/2026/08/04/msr-92nd-anniversary-cecil-newman-legacy-2/)). Insight News publishes from 1815 Bryant Avenue North ([Insight News](https://www.insightnews.com/)). Its own site could not be reached.

source.heading: All walks of life
source.body:
All figures in this section come from the Compass 2020 to 2024 profile, in 2024 dollars, unless another source is named ([Minnesota Compass](https://www.mncompass.org/topics/demographics/cultural-communities/minnesota)).

- **Comfortable and wealthy households.** The median household income is $86,893, give or take $560, and 43.6 percent of the state's 2,307,855 households take in $100,000 or more. At the very top, Forbes' 2025 list counted five Minnesota billionaires. Glen Taylor led them at $2.9 billion. He bought a wedding service business for $2 million in 1975 and built it into the printing company Taylor Corp; Jeffrey Michael and Stanley Hubbard of Hubbard Broadcasting were also on the list ([KROC News, April 6, 2025](https://krocnews.com/five-minnesotans-now-on-world-billionaires-list-in-2025/); [KROC News, July 19, 2025](https://krocnews.com/this-billionaire-is-minnesotas-richest-person-in-2025/)).
- **Professionals and owners.** Among adults 25 and older, 39.3 percent hold a bachelor's degree or more, including 13.7 percent with a graduate or professional degree. The state is home to 17 companies on the 2025 Fortune 500, led by UnitedHealth Group at No. 3 ([Twin Cities Business, 2025](https://tcbmag.com/fortune-500-list-contains-some-warnings-for-minnesota/)). Small firms dominate by count: a KROC report on large employers noted that more than 94 percent of Minnesota businesses employ fewer than 50 people ([KROC News, 2025](https://krocnews.com/here-are-the-five-largest-employers-in-minnesota-in-2025/)).
- **Middle-income and working families.** Owners occupy 72.4 percent of homes. Among adults 18 to 64, 80.2 percent are employed: 82.4 percent of men and 78.0 percent of women. Another 12.9 percent of people live between the poverty line and twice that line. Costs press on these families. The Economic Policy Institute put average infant care at more than $22,000 a year in 2025, behind only Washington, D.C., and Massachusetts ([Center for Rural Policy and Development, quoting Minnesota Reformer, March 15, 2025](https://www.ruralmn.org/minnesota-reformer-child-care-costs-more-in-minnesota-than-almost-any-other-state-study-finds/)).
- **People in poverty or close to it.** Statewide, 8.1 percent of people live below the poverty line, including 8.9 percent of children and 16.1 percent of 18- to 24-year-olds, many of them students. Among renters, 47.4 percent spend too much of their income on housing, compared with 19.0 percent of owners. Median rent is $1,280. Minnesotans made 9,026,843 visits to food shelves in 2025, the fourth record year in a row and about 2.5 times the 2019 level, The Food Group reported. It found that 83 percent of monthly users now come more than once a month ([MPR News, March 18, 2026](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2026/03/18/minnesotans-made-9-million-visits-to-food-shelves-in-2025)). Second Harvest Heartland distributed a record 172 million pounds of food in its 2026 fiscal year and named the federal immigration surge, inflation and diesel prices among the causes ([MPR News, Oct. 17, 2026](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2026/10/17/record-172-million-pounds-of-food-distributed-to-food-shelves-amid-high-inflation)).

**Gaps inside the mainstream.** The same averages hide large differences by race. The Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis found Black homeownership in the Twin Cities fell to 29 percent in 2024, the widest Black-white gap of any comparable metro, at 46.9 points ([CBS Minnesota, May 10, 2026](https://www.cbsnews.com/minnesota/news/black-homeownership-twin-cities-gap-minneapolis-federal-reserve/)). A Minnesota Housing official traced the gap in part to racial covenants and decades of unequal wealth building ([KTTC, June 17, 2026](https://www.kttc.com/2026/06/17/minnesota-black-homeownership-gap-rooted-racial-covenants/)). Health coverage shows a similar pattern (section 11).

findings: 2024 dollars applies to financial amounts, not percentages. Clarify percentage-point gap; preserve all numerical values.

source.heading: Health and wellbeing, broadly
source.body:
**Insurance through work, government, or not at all.** Coverage in Minnesota runs mainly through employers and public programs. The Minnesota Health Access Survey found 51.4 percent of Minnesotans covered through an employer in 2025, up from 49.3 percent in 2023. Public coverage (Medical Assistance, MinnesotaCare, Medicare, Tricare) fell from 44.1 to 39.6 percent, and individually bought coverage held at 3.2 percent. The uninsured rate rose from a record low of 3.8 percent in 2023 to 5.8 percent in 2025, about 116,000 more people. source.heading: Disability
source.body:
**How many.** Compass counts 11.7 percent of Minnesotans with a disability, and 8.3 percent of those under 65 ([Minnesota Compass](https://www.mncompass.org/topics/demographics/cultural-communities/minnesota)).

**Work.** The Minnesota Council on Disability reports a 2023 employment rate of 22.5 percent for people with disabilities against 65.8 percent for people without, and an unemployment rate of 7.2 percent against 3.5 percent ([Minnesota Council on Disability](https://www.disability.state.mn.us/technical-assistance/employment/)).

**Subminimum wages: a live disagreement.** Section 14(c) of the federal Fair Labor Standards Act, passed in 1938, allows people with disabilities to be paid less than the minimum wage, The Arc Minnesota notes. The Metropolitan Center for Independent Living estimates about 3,500 Minnesotans earn around $4 an hour, often for about 10 hours a week, in segregated settings ([MCIL](https://mcil-mn.org/minnesota-disability-employment-statistics/)). The Arc Minnesota backed a 2025 bill, SF 2149, to end the practice by 2028 and called it "archaic and discriminatory" ([The Arc Minnesota testimony, March 10, 2025](https://www.lrl.mn.gov/archive/minutes/senate/2025/labor/20250311/labor_20250311_sf2149-testimony-The-Arc-Minnesota.pdf)). Letters to a 2024 Senate committee came from parents and providers on the side of ending it. One provider wrote that opponents say the change would ruin people's lives, and a parent who supported the bill wrote that for people in day programs, work should be a choice, not a requirement ([Senate committee letters, March 2024](https://www.lrl.mn.gov/archive/minutes/senate/2024/human/20240318/Human_20240318_SF4399-Combined-Letters.pdf)). As checked for this page, the state minimum wage statute contains no phase-out date ([Minn. Stat. 177.24](https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/177.24)).

**Community living.** Minnesota's Olmstead Plan, named for the 1999 U.S. Supreme Court decision and required by the Jensen settlement, sets goals for disabled Minnesotans to live integrated lives in communities of their choosing. A revised plan was being drafted in 2026, and MCIL and ADA Minnesota submitted comments on education and employment ([MCIL](https://mcil-mn.org/mcil-ada-minnesota-submits-comments-on-education-and-employment-to-minnesota-olmstead-plan/)).

**When a program ends.** The Department of Human Services ended Housing Stabilization Services, a Medicaid program launched in 2020 to help older adults, people with disabilities and people with mental illness or addiction find and keep housing, after federal prosecutors charged eight people with stealing about $10 million from it ([Yahoo News/Pioneer Press, Oct. 31, 2025](https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/minnesota-ends-medicaid-funded-housing-214200017.html)). DHS's commissioner and inspector general said fraud left no choice. A Republican legislator called the shutdown "too little, too late" and said it penalized "the people who needed it most" ([KAAL](https://www.kaaltv.com/news/minnesota-dhs-moves-to-terminate-housing-stabilization-services-program-amid-fraud-concerns/)). How many disabled Minnesotans lost help, and what replaced it, could not be confirmed.

**Everyday access.** Mainstream consumer life is adding accommodations. Mall of America's site, for example, has accessibility and sensory-friendly resource pages ([Mall of America](https://www.mallofamerica.com/about)).

**Questions this page leaves open.** Do survey counts match how people see themselves? Who in Minnesota decides that a person counts as disabled: a doctor, a county assessor, the census question, or the person? What does the label open, such as waivers or workplace accommodation, and what does it close, such as a full wage under 14(c)? How much disability among veterans, older adults and workers in physical jobs comes from service, aging or injury? No Minnesota source opened for this page answered these by group, and they should stay questions.

findings: 2023 employment figures are national BLS data, not Minnesota estimates. Confirmed against BLS primary release.
Section 14(c) requires employer certificate and specific work-related conditions; disability status alone does not authorize subminimum wage. Confirmed DOL primary source.
Current program closure/Olmstead chronology and state wage-law claims need separately checked source scope before whole-record acceptance.

source.heading: Work and the economy
source.body:
**The job market.** Minnesota's unemployment rate was 4.5 percent in September 2026, above the national 4.2 percent. Its labor force participation rate, 66.7 percent, was well above the national 61.8 percent ([DEED, September 2026 Employment Analysis](https://mn.gov/deed/assets/Sep%202026%20Employment%20Analysis_final_tcm1045-283140.pdf)). In the 12 months to July 2026 the state added 44,092 jobs, growth of 1.5 percent against 0.2 percent nationally ([KTTC, Aug. 20, 2026](https://www.kttc.com/2026/08/20/minnesota-annual-job-growth-outpaces-rest-us/)).

**Where people work.** Health care and social assistance is the largest employing industry, with 556,992 jobs in 2025, about 18.9 percent of all jobs. It accounted for about 55.8 percent of the state's job growth from 2015 to 2025, the state's CareerForce site reports ([CareerForce, DEED](https://careerforce.mn.gov/industry/health-care)). Mayo Clinic is the largest single employer, with 56,999 Minnesota employees in KROC's 2025 count ([KROC News, 2025](https://krocnews.com/here-are-the-five-largest-employers-in-minnesota-in-2025/)). The 2025 Fortune 500 list included UnitedHealth Group, Target, U.S. Bancorp, Best Buy, CHS, 3M, General Mills, Ameriprise, C.H. Robinson, Land O'Lakes, Ecolab, Xcel Energy, Hormel, Thrivent, Solventum, Securian and Fastenal. About half saw revenue fall in fiscal 2024 ([Twin Cities Business](https://tcbmag.com/fortune-500-list-contains-some-warnings-for-minnesota/)).

**Labor history and unions.** Unions are part of the American story here. St. Paul tailors struck in 1854, and the city's printers formed the state's first lasting union in 1856. From 1900 to 1910, about 30,000 people marched in St. Paul's Labor Day parade each year and picnicked on Harriet Island. The Teamsters' 1934 coal drivers' and truckers' strikes challenged an employers' alliance that had blocked organizing in Minneapolis, and public employees here became national leaders in winning union recognition, MNopedia records ([MNopedia, Labor and Labor Organizing in Minnesota](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/labor-and-labor-organizing-minnesota)). The Bureau of Labor Statistics put Minnesota's union membership rate at 14.2 percent in 2024, 11th highest in the country, against 9.9 percent nationally ([Minneapolis Regional Labor Federation, Feb. 28, 2025](https://minneapolisunions.org/news/mlr2025-02-28-union-members-grew-in-MN)).

**The rules of work, as Minnesota writes them.** Workplace norms that feel "normal" are often set in law:
- The state minimum wage is $11.41 an hour in 2026 and rises to $11.87 on Jan. 1, 2027 ([Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry](https://www.dli.mn.gov/minwage)).
- Workers earn at least one hour of sick and safe time for every 30 hours worked, up to 48 hours a year ([Minn. Stat. 181.9446](https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/181.9446)).
- Noncompete clauses in employment agreements are void ([Minn. Stat. 181.988](https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/181.988)).
- Employees may leave work long enough to vote, on Election Day or during in-person early voting, without penalty or loss of pay ([Minn. Stat. 204C.04](https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/204C.04)).
- Minnesota Paid Leave began Jan. 1, 2026. In its first six months it drew about 100,000 applications and approved roughly 75,000, paying about $600 million. The average weekly benefit was about $1,083, and medical and bonding leave were most common, a DEED deputy commissioner said ([KTTC, July 7, 2026](https://www.kttc.com/2026/07/07/first-6-months-mn-paid-leave-program-draws-100000-applications/)). Not everyone agrees with it. The Republican candidate for governor, the Speaker of the Minnesota House, has called the mandate "a tax on every business" and wants to roll it back ([MultiState](https://www.multistate.us/elections/governor-race/minnesota-2026)).

**The office.** In 2025 large employers pulled office staff back. 3M required non-production workers on site at least four days a week from September 2025 ([KSTP, 2025](https://kstp.com/kstp-news/local-news/3m-to-bring-employees-back-to-office-4-days-a-week-starting-in-september/)). Target asked several departments to come in three days a week, General Mills moved to a Tuesday-through-Thursday schedule, and the Minneapolis Downtown Council estimated peak weekday downtown crowds at about 70 percent of the pre-pandemic level ([Twin Cities Business, July 10, 2025](https://tcbmag.com/target-issues-return-to-office-orders/)). In the Compass profile, 76.5 percent of workers get to work by car, truck or van, 2.0 percent by public transit, and 21.5 percent walk, bike, work at home or use other means ([Minnesota Compass](https://www.mncompass.org/topics/demographics/cultural-communities/minnesota)).

**Unpaid work.** In 2023, 40.3 percent of Minnesotans, about 1.8 million people, volunteered through an organization, third in the country behind Utah and Vermont, according to AmeriCorps data reported by InForum ([InForum, 2024](https://www.inforum.com/news/moorhead/minnesota-ranks-3rd-for-volunteering-as-national-rates-rebound-post-pandemic-study-shows)).

findings: Blanket noncompete, sick-time and paid-leave statements need legal scope/effective-date verification. Do not polish over exceptions.
Do not change about 55.8 to nearly 55.8 or suggest all workplace norms result from state law.

In the 12 months to July 2026 the state added 44,092 jobs, growth of 1.5 percent against 0.2 percent nationally ([KTTC, Aug. 20, 2026](https://www.kttc.com/2026/08/20/minnesota-annual-job-growth-outpaces-rest-us/)).

**Where people work.** Health care and social assistance is the largest employing industry, with 556,992 jobs in 2025, about 18.9 percent of all jobs. It accounted for about 55.8 percent of the state's job growth from 2015 to 2025, the state's CareerForce site reports ([CareerForce, DEED](https://careerforce.mn.gov/industry/health-care)). Mayo Clinic is the largest single employer, with 56,999 Minnesota employees in KROC's 2025 count ([KROC News, 2025](https://krocnews.com/here-are-the-five-largest-employers-in-minnesota-in-2025/)). The 2025 Fortune 500 list included UnitedHealth Group, Target, U.S. Bancorp, Best Buy, CHS, 3M, General Mills, Ameriprise, C.H. Robinson, Land O'Lakes, Ecolab, Xcel Energy, Hormel, Thrivent, Solventum, Securian and Fastenal. About half saw revenue fall in fiscal 2024 ([Twin Cities Business](https://tcbmag.com/fortune-500-list-contains-some-warnings-for-minnesota/)).

**Labor history and unions.** Unions are part of the American story here. St. Paul tailors struck in 1854, and the city's printers formed the state's first lasting union in 1856. From 1900 to 1910, about 30,000 people marched in St. Paul's Labor Day parade each year and picnicked on Harriet Island. The Teamsters' 1934 coal drivers' and truckers' strikes challenged an employers' alliance that had blocked organizing in Minneapolis, and public employees here became national leaders in winning union recognition, MNopedia records ([MNopedia, Labor and Labor Organizing in Minnesota](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/labor-and-labor-organizing-minnesota)). The Bureau of Labor Statistics put Minnesota's union membership rate at 14.2 percent in 2024, 11th highest in the country, against 9.9 percent nationally ([Minneapolis Regional Labor Federation, Feb. 28, 2025](https://minneapolisunions.org/news/mlr2025-02-28-union-members-grew-in-MN)).

**The rules of work, as Minnesota writes them.** Some workplace expectations are legal requirements. Their scope and exceptions matter:
- The state minimum wage is $11.41 an hour in 2026 and rises to $11.87 on Jan. 1, 2027 ([Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry](https://www.dli.mn.gov/minwage)).
- Employees covered by Minnesota’s earned sick and safe time law generally accrue at least one hour for every 30 hours worked, up to 48 hours a year under the accrual method unless the employer permits a higher amount. Coverage generally includes employees anticipated to work at least 80 hours in a year for the employer in Minnesota; the law also permits specified front-loading arrangements ([Minnesota DLI](https://dli.mn.gov/sick-leave)) ([Minn. Stat. 181.9446](https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/181.9446)).
- Minnesota generally bars employment noncompete agreements entered into on or after July 1, 2023, with specified exceptions for a business sale or dissolution. The statute distinguishes noncompetes from nondisclosure and nonsolicitation agreements ([Minn. Stat. 181.988](https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/181.988)).
- Employees may leave work long enough to vote, on Election Day or during in-person early voting, without penalty or loss of pay ([Minn. Stat. 204C.04](https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/204C.04)).
- Minnesota Paid Leave began Jan. 1, 2026. In its first six months it drew about 100,000 applications and approved roughly 75,000, paying about $600 million. The average weekly benefit was about $1,083, and medical and bonding leave were most common, a DEED deputy commissioner said ([KTTC, July 7, 2026](https://www.kttc.com/2026/07/07/first-6-months-mn-paid-leave-program-draws-100000-applications/)). Not everyone agrees with it. The Republican candidate for governor, the Speaker of the Minnesota House, has called the mandate "a tax on every business" and wants to roll it back ([MultiState](https://www.multistate.us/elections/governor-race/minnesota-2026)).

**The office.** In 2025 large employers pulled office staff back. 3M required non-production workers on site at least four days a week from September 2025 ([KSTP, 2025](https://kstp.com/kstp-news/local-news/3m-to-bring-employees-back-to-office-4-days-a-week-starting-in-september/)). Target asked several departments to come in three days a week, General Mills moved to a Tuesday-through-Thursday schedule, and the Minneapolis Downtown Council estimated peak weekday downtown crowds at about 70 percent of the pre-pandemic level ([Twin Cities Business, July 10, 2025](https://tcbmag.com/target-issues-return-to-office-orders/)). In the Compass profile, 76.5 percent of workers get to work by car, truck or van, 2.0 percent by public transit, and 21.5 percent walk, bike, work at home or use other means ([Minnesota Compass](https://www.mncompass.org/topics/demographics/cultural-communities/minnesota)).

**Unpaid work.** In 2023, 40.3 percent of Minnesotans, about 1.8 million people, volunteered through an organization, third in the country behind Utah and Vermont, according to AmeriCorps data reported by InForum ([InForum, 2024](https://www.inforum.com/news/moorhead/minnesota-ranks-3rd-for-volunteering-as-national-rates-rebound-post-pandemic-study-shows)).

source.heading: Businesses and commercial life
source.body:
Mainstream American commercial life, from the enclosed mall to the big-box store, has deep Minnesota roots. The list of businesses checked for this page is in the accompanying businesses file. Here are the main threads.

**America's first indoor mall.** Southdale Center in Edina, which a Minnesota Historical Society video on MNopedia calls "America's First Indoor Mall," opened on Oct. 8, 1956, with 72 stores and two anchors. About 75,000 people came to the opening. Dayton's department store hired designer Victor Gruen after a study found only 126 "ideal shopping weather" days a year ([MNopedia, Southdale Center](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/structure/southdale-center)). Mall of America in Bloomington opened in 1992 on the old Metropolitan Stadium site with 330 stores. It reports 32 million visitors a year and more than $3 billion in yearly economic impact ([Mall of America, About](https://www.mallofamerica.com/about)). It hosted a free Minnesota America 250 exhibit and ceremony over the July 4, 2026 weekend ([Dakota County](https://dakotacountymn.gov/government/news/america-250-event-to-be-held-at-mall-of-america)).

**National brands with local headquarters.** Target, Best Buy, General Mills and 3M are among the household names based here (section 3). Grocery shopping runs through chains such as Cub and Lunds & Byerlys. Holiday Stationstores now operates under Circle K, whose parent company is named on Holiday's site ([Holiday Stationstores](https://www.holidaystationstores.com/)). Hormel's SPAM Museum in Austin is open daily ([SPAM Museum](https://www.spam.com/museum)).

**American food, Minnesota style.** Minneapolis's Matt's Bar has served the cheese-stuffed "Jucy Lucy" burger since the 1950s and spells it without the "i" on purpose ([Matt's Bar](https://mattsbar.com/)). The 5-8 Club serves its own "Juicy Lucy" at four locations ([5-8 Club](https://www.5-8club.com/)). Steakhouses such as Murray's in downtown Minneapolis, Manny's, Jax Cafe in Northeast Minneapolis (dating to 1933) and Mancini's Char House in St. Paul keep an older dining style alive ([Murray's](https://www.murraysrestaurant.com/); [Jax Cafe](https://www.jaxcafe.com/); [Mancini's](https://mancinis.com/)). Minnesota raises more turkeys than any other state, 32.0 million in 2025, which puts it at the center of the Thanksgiving table ([USDA NASS, Sept. 26, 2025](https://www.nass.usda.gov/Publications/Todays_Reports/reports/tuky0925.pdf)).

**The State Fair as a marketplace.** The Minnesota State Fair is part agricultural show, part food court, part shopping mall. It drew 1,923,325 people over 12 days from Aug. 27 to Sept. 7, 2026. Its competitions drew more than 38,000 entries and nearly $2.5 million in prize money ([Minnesota State Fair](https://www.mnstatefair.org/updates/2026-fair)).

**Business groups and media.** The Minnesota Chamber of Commerce, the St. Paul Area Chamber and the Minneapolis Regional Chamber all keep current 2026 websites ([Minnesota Chamber](https://www.mnchamber.com/); [St. Paul Area Chamber](https://www.saintpaulchamber.com/); [Minneapolis Regional Chamber](https://www.minneapolischamber.org/)). Mainstream news reaches Minnesotans through MPR News, the Star Tribune, the Pioneer Press, KARE 11, KSTP, FOX 9 and CBS Minnesota (WCCO), along with Twin Cities Business, Minnesota Monthly and Mpls.St.Paul Magazine.

**How deep this list goes.** The businesses file is a sample of mainstream institutions and landmarks, not a directory. Countless ordinary firms make up this part of the economy, and listing them would not describe a culture.

source.heading: Religion and spiritual life
source.body:
**What the numbers show.** Pew Research Center's 2023-24 Religious Landscape Study describes Minnesota adults this way: 22 percent mainline Protestant, 20 percent evangelical Protestant, 18 percent Catholic, 1 percent in historically Black Protestant churches, 3 percent Muslim, and smaller shares of other faiths. Lutherans of all kinds make up about 23 percent: 16 percent in mainline Lutheran bodies, including 12 percent in the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America (ELCA), and 7 percent in evangelical Lutheran bodies, including 5 percent in the Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod. The religiously unaffiliated make up 29 percent: 5 percent atheist, 9 percent agnostic and 15 percent "nothing in particular." Pew gives a margin of error of 5.7 points for Minnesota ([Pew Research Center](https://www.pewresearch.org/religious-landscape-study/state/minnesota/)). In short, Minnesota's mainstream is still mostly Christian, unusually Lutheran, and home to a large group of people with no religion.

**Older churches are shrinking.** A 2018 report covered by Patch found the ELCA had nearly 200,000 fewer Minnesota members than in 2000 and had lost about 150 churches, with more than 1,000 of its remaining churches under 50 members. Catholic numbers held steady, but about 80 Catholic churches had closed since 2000. The decline reached rural, suburban and urban churches alike ([Patch, July 9, 2018](https://patch.com/minnesota/southwestminneapolis/minnesota-churches-are-steep-decline-report)). Newer figures for the state could not be opened.

**Where growth shows.** Large nondenominational churches are part of the mainstream too. Eagle Brook Church lists 14 campuses across Minnesota plus online services and posted new messages through October 2026 ([Eagle Brook Church](https://www.eaglebrookchurch.com/)). The Archdiocese of Saint Paul and Minneapolis, Temple Israel in Minneapolis and many other congregations post current schedules ([Archdiocese](https://www.archspm.org/); [Temple Israel](https://www.templeisrael.com/)).

**Sunday, sports and family time.** One tension inside mainstream family life is between worship and weekend activities. In August 2025 the Archdiocese of Saint Paul and Minneapolis launched "Reclaiming Sundays," a year-long guide and video series that suggests themes such as screen-free Sundays to help families keep the day for prayer and rest, Archbishop Bernard Hebda said ([National Catholic Register/CNA, Aug. 27, 2025](https://www.ncregister.com/cna/catholic-families-reclaim-the-sabbath)).

**Civil religion.** Some public rituals of national loyalty are written into law. Minnesota law requires every public school to display the U.S. flag, and public and charter school students recite the Pledge of Allegiance at least once a week. Any student or teacher may decline, and handbooks must say so. A school board can vote to waive the weekly recitation ([Minn. Stat. 121A.11](https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/121A.11)). On July 8, 2026, the Governor's Committee for Minnesota America 250 and the Minnesota Historical Society held a public reading of the Declaration of Independence in the State Capitol rotunda ([Minnesota Historical Society, July 1, 2026](https://www.mnhs.org/media/news/commemorate-americas-250th-anniversary-fourth-july)).

> **Content note:** This passage describes the 2025 shooting at Annunciation Catholic Church, in which two children were killed. Readers may skip to the next paragraph.

**Faith and tragedy.** On Aug. 27, 2025, a gunman fired into Annunciation Catholic Church in Minneapolis during a school Mass, killing two children and injuring 28 other people, MPR News reported. Afterward, parents organized, the church's new pastor helped children with questions about life, death and God, and gun bills were introduced at the Capitol ([MPR News, Annunciation coverage](https://www.mprnews.org/annunciation-catholic-church-and-school-shooting/3)).

**People of no faith.** The 29 percent who are unaffiliated still take part in the civic calendar, holidays and rites of passage described here. Pew's Minnesota page does not break down how they mark weddings or funerals, and no Minnesota source on that question was found.

findings: Unaffiliated does not necessarily mean no religion or no faith. Do not infer civic observance for every unaffiliated individual.

source.heading: Celebrations and observances
source.body:
Minnesota law names the legal holidays on which public business stops: New Year's Day (Jan. 1); Martin Luther King's Birthday (third Monday in January); Washington's and Lincoln's Birthday (third Monday in February); Memorial Day (last Monday in May); Juneteenth (June 19); Independence Day (July 4); Labor Day (first Monday in September); Indigenous Peoples Day (second Monday in October); Veterans Day (Nov. 11); Thanksgiving (fourth Thursday in November); and Christmas (Dec. 25). When a fixed-date holiday falls on a Sunday, Monday is the holiday; on a Saturday, Friday is. The state's executive branch also closes the Friday after Thanksgiving but does not close on Indigenous Peoples Day. Other branches, counties and cities choose for themselves ([Minn. Stat. 645.44, subd. 5](https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/645.44)). The calendar file lists dates for 2026 to 2028.

- **New Year's Day.** A legal holiday by statute. No Minnesota-specific public tradition was documented for this page.
- **Martin Luther King Jr. Day.** General Mills and UNCF held the 36th annual Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Holiday Breakfast at the Minneapolis Convention Center on Jan. 19, 2026, with Soledad O'Brien and Freeman Hrabowski as keynote speakers ([General Mills, Dec. 16, 2025](https://www.generalmills.com/news-and-stories/press-releases/general-mills-and-uncf-celebrate-36th-annual-dr-martin-luther-king-jr-holiday-breakfast)). Colleges such as St. Olaf hold a month of events ([St. Olaf College](https://wp.stolaf.edu/mlkday/)). The African American page covers the day's deeper meaning.
- **Washington's and Lincoln's Birthday.** Often called Presidents' Day. Minnesota law keeps the older name ([Minn. Stat. 645.44](https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/645.44)).
- **St. Patrick's Day.** St. Paul held its 60th annual parade on March 17, 2026, from Mears Park along Fifth Street to Rice Park, led by the year's Miss Shamrock. MPR described the crowd as "green-clad Irish and Irish wannabes" ([MPR News, March 17, 2026](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2026/03/17/thousands-march-through-st-paul-in-60th-st-patricks-day-parade)).
- **Easter.** A major Christian feast. It is not a state legal holiday. No Minnesota-wide public observance was documented for this page beyond congregations' own services.
- **Memorial Day.** Fort Snelling National Cemetery hosts a wreath-laying with music, speeches, a rifle volley and Taps, and the governor usually speaks. In 2025 it began at 9:45 a.m. ([KTTC, May 26, 2025](https://www.kttc.com/2025/05/26/fort-snelling-hold-wreath-laying-ceremony-memorial-day/)).
- **Juneteenth.** The governor signed the bill making Juneteenth a state holiday on Feb. 3, 2023 ([MPR News, Feb. 3, 2023](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2023/02/03/juneteenth-is-now-a-holiday-in-minnesota)). The African American page covers community celebrations.
- **Independence Day.** In 2026 the holiday marked the nation's 250th anniversary. Because July 4 fell on a Saturday, many people had Friday off. Events ranged from the Minneapolis Park Board's Red, White and Boom! on the riverfront to small-town parades in Delano, Ely and Stillwater ([MPR News, June 26, 2026](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2026/06/26/fourth-of-july-events-guide-fireworks-parades-in-minnesota); [FOX 9, June 30, 2026](https://www.fox9.com/news/things-do-minnesota-5-things-do-fourth-july-weekend-2026)). Historic Fort Snelling and the Oliver Kelley Farm held historical celebrations ([Minnesota Historical Society](https://www.mnhs.org/media/news/commemorate-americas-250th-anniversary-fourth-july)).
- **Labor Day.** For many Minnesotans the holiday is the last day of the State Fair, which runs for the 12 days ending on Labor Day ([Minnesota State Fair](https://www.mnstatefair.org/updates/2026-fair)). The first fair was held in 1859, and the fair moved to its permanent grounds between St. Paul and Minneapolis in 1885 ([MNopedia](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/event/minnesota-state-fair-origins-and-traditions)). Public schools generally may not start until after Labor Day ([Minn. Stat. 120A.40](https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/120A.40)).
- **Indigenous Peoples Day.** Minnesota law has named the second Monday in October Indigenous Peoples Day, replacing Columbus Day in public-employer contracts ([Minn. Stat. 645.44](https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/645.44)). This page does not go further. That history belongs with the Tribal Nations and the offices that serve them.
- **Halloween.** Anoka calls itself the "Halloween Capital of the World." Its organizers say civic leaders started a citywide celebration in 1920 to keep young people from pranks ([Anoka Halloween, history](https://anokahalloween.com/history/)). The 2026 Grande Day Parade ran on Main Street on Saturday, Oct. 24, from 1 to 3:30 p.m. ([Anoka Halloween](https://anokahalloween.com/event/grande-day-parade/)).
- **Election Day.** Minnesota's general election is Nov. 3, 2026. By Oct. 16, election officials had accepted 202,252 absentee ballots, 17 percent more than at the same point in 2022 ([KAXE, Oct. 19, 2026](https://www.kaxe.org/elections/2026-10-19/early-voting-opens-in-mn-midterms-as-absentee-ballots-roll-in)). Workers have a legal right to time off to vote (section 3).
- **Veterans Day.** The state's official program has been held in Inver Grove Heights, with a breakfast for veterans and families and music by the 34th Infantry Division Red Bull Band ([CBS Minnesota](https://www.cbsnews.com/minnesota/news/hundreds-gather-at-state-veterans-day-program/)).
- **Thanksgiving.** Each year the governor welcomes an official Thanksgiving turkey to the Capitol with the Minnesota Turkey Growers Association, honoring the state's more than 600 turkey farms ([WDIO](https://www.wdio.com/top-stories/minnesota-turkey-showcased-at-the-state-capitol/)).
- **Christmas.** A Christian feast and a legal holiday. In Duluth, Bentleyville "Tour of Lights" calls itself America's largest free walk-through lighting display and runs Nov. 21 to Dec. 26, 2026, its 23rd season ([Bentleyville](https://www.bentleyvilleusa.org/)).

findings: Holiday weekend substitution applies to specified fixed-date holidays, not an unrestricted all-holidays rule; verify statutory wording before correction.
2026 election date should be described historically, without a claim about turnout/results.

source.heading: Family, home and daily life
source.body:
**Households.** Compass counts 2,307,855 households averaging 2.41 people. Married couples without children under 18 make up 30.0 percent, married couples with children 19.1 percent, single mothers with children 3.7 percent, single fathers 1.2 percent, and unmarried couples 8.0 percent. People living alone are 29.9 percent of households ([Minnesota Compass](https://www.mncompass.org/topics/demographics/cultural-communities/minnesota)). The "typical" two-parent family with children is about one household in five.

**Fewer children.** "We haven't had replacement level fertility in Minnesota since 2006," state demographer Megan Dayton told Twin Cities Business. The state's birth rate fell from 14.16 per 1,000 people in 2007 to 11.71 in 2019, and demographers projected deaths would outnumber births around 2040 ([Twin Cities Business, 2021](https://tcbmag.com/what-a-declining-u-s-birth-rate-could-mean-for-minnesota/)). Newer state birth figures could not be opened. Child care costs (section 2) are one pressure that families name.

**Cars and commutes.** Most households have a car: 39.4 percent have two and 23.1 percent have three or more, while 6.6 percent have none. Almost half of workers who leave home get to work in under 20 minutes, and 28.7 percent travel 30 minutes or more ([Minnesota Compass](https://www.mncompass.org/topics/demographics/cultural-communities/minnesota)).

**Food.** Minnesota supplies 16 percent of all U.S. turkeys, with turkey making up 61 percent of the state's poultry production, according to the governor's office ([WDIO](https://www.wdio.com/top-stories/minnesota-turkey-showcased-at-the-state-capitol/)). Schools in the national lunch program must take part in the state's free school meals program, and schools may not shame or single out a student who owes money for meals ([Minn. Stat. 124D.111](https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/124D.111)).

**Childhood.** Organized activities reach a large share of teenagers. In 2024-25, 232,347 students took part in Minnesota State High School League athletics, 10th most in the country. Adding fine arts activities and robotics brought participation to an all-time high of 277,773 ([MSHSL, Aug. 19, 2025](https://www.mshsl.org/about/news/league-news/mshsl-maintains-spot-top-10-nfhs-annual-participation-survey)). At the State Fair, 115 4-H members sold livestock in the 2026 Purple Ribbon Auction, which raised more than $1.35 million ([Minnesota State Fair](https://www.mnstatefair.org/updates/2026-fair)).

**Aging.** People 65 and older are 17.3 percent of Minnesotans. Poverty in that age group is 7.9 percent, slightly below the statewide rate ([Minnesota Compass](https://www.mncompass.org/topics/demographics/cultural-communities/minnesota)).

**Weddings, dress, divorce.** No Minnesota-specific source on wedding customs, dress norms or divorce was opened for this page. National patterns should not be assumed to describe any one family.

findings: 19.1 percent refers to married-couple households with children, not every two-parent family.
MSHSL participation totals may count repeat participation across activities, not distinct students; source access was denied, so do not certify the denominator.
Reject candidate often mention child-care costs; frequency not established.

source.heading: Arts, media, sports and culture
source.body:
**Minnesota's place in American literature and music.** Sauk Centre's Sinclair Lewis wrote *Main Street* (1920), set in a fictional version of his hometown. It sold 180,000 copies in just over six months, and Lewis became the first American to win the Nobel Prize in Literature ([MNopedia](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/person/lewis-harry-sinclair-1885-1951)). Prince, born in Minneapolis in 1958 and raised on the Northside, is credited by MNopedia as the main creator of the Minneapolis Sound ([MNopedia](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/person/prince-1958-2016)).

**Big-league sports.** The Twins brought major-league baseball to Minnesota in 1961, and the Vikings played their first season the same year at Metropolitan Stadium. The Timberwolves began in 1989, the Lynx in 1999 (winning four WNBA titles in seven years in the 2010s), and the Wild in 2000 ([MNopedia, Minnesota sports](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/gophers-vikings-and-saints-highlights-history-minnesota-sports)). The Minnesota Frost won the first two championships of the Professional Women's Hockey League, in 2024 and 2025 ([MPR News, May 26, 2025](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2025/05/26/minnesota-frost-beat-ottawa-charge-2-1-game-4)).

**School sports as community life.** MNopedia calls Minnesota "a natural leader" in girls' and women's hockey: the state high school league sanctioned girls' hockey as a varsity sport after the 1993-94 season, and the first official season began in November 1994 ([MNopedia](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/gophers-vikings-and-saints-highlights-history-minnesota-sports)). The boys' state hockey tournament, called "The Tourney," was held in March 2026 at the renamed Grand Casino Arena, formerly the Xcel Energy Center ([Post Bulletin, March 4, 2026](https://www.postbulletin.com/sports/prep/all-you-need-to-know-about-the-tourney-the-2026-minnesota-boys-hockey-state-tournament)). Its 2025 Class AA final drew 20,491 fans, more than the average NHL game that season ([ESPN Sioux Falls, March 11, 2025](https://espnsiouxfalls.com/ixp/65/p/prep-hockey-championship-draws-more-fans-than-a-nhl-game/)).

**Fairs, history and arts.** The State Fair's Fine Arts Exhibition, the largest juried art show in Minnesota, drew 3,185 submissions in 2026 and accepted 343 ([Minnesota State Fair](https://www.mnstatefair.org/updates/2026-fair)). For the nation's 250th anniversary, the Minnesota Historical Society offered "MN250" road trips through what it calls "all-American stories" at its historic sites ([Minnesota Historical Society, MN250](https://www.mnhs.org/mn250)).

**Media.** The state's main news outlets are listed in section 4. Several, such as the Pioneer Press and Minnesota Public Radio, are long-standing Minnesota institutions.

findings: Original arts account gives concrete institutions, historical context, and dates in readable professional prose. Retain original editorially; model replacements offer no substantive benefit.

The soccer federation nearly moved its tournament because members were afraid ([MPR News, June 30, 2026](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2026/06/30/ethiopian-soccer-tournament-draws-thousands-despite-immigration-fears)). The Ethiopian page covers the end of Temporary Protected Status for Ethiopia.
- **War again, October 2026.** Fighting in Tigray and continuing conflict in the Amhara region (section 9) reach Amharic-speaking families here through relatives, news and social media. No Minnesota reporting on that reaction was found.
- **New church buildings.** Debre Selam Medhanealem opened its Seward church in April 2026; Debre Bisrat's new Rosemount church burned in July (Ethiopian page).
- **Language policy.** Minnesota's Enterprise Translations Office, created in 2023 to standardize translation across about 25 state agencies, had two staff each for Spanish, Hmong and Somali as of September 2025, and its budget to reimburse outside translation had been cut from $250,000 to $100,000 a year ([Sahan Journal, Sept. 22, 2025](https://sahanjournal.com/immigration/minnesota-non-english-languages-census-data/)). The report names no Amharic translators on the office's staff.
- **Generations.** Heritage language licenses, bilingual seals and English youth services all point to a community deciding how to keep Amharic while its children grow up in English.

source.heading: Work and the economy
source.body:
There is no Minnesota data on what Amharic speakers do for a living. A few kinds of work are tied directly to the language.

**Interpreting.** Interpreting is paid work that depends on the language, and Minnesota sets few rules for it. The Minnesota Department of Health keeps a voluntary roster of spoken-language health care interpreters. Listing requires no proof of skill, the department says it is not authorized to verify what interpreters report, and some insurers require roster listing in order to bill ([MDH](https://www.health.state.mn.us/facilities/providers/interpreter/index.html)). In a 2015 report to the Legislature, MDH said the roster grew from about 100 interpreters in January 2010 to about 3,600 by December 2014, across 225 languages. An Amharic and Oromo interpreter quoted in that report objected to enforcement against interpreters and said pay in medical interpreting was low ([MDH, Interpreting in Health Care Settings, 2015, via Legislative Reference Library](https://www.lrl.mn.gov/docs/2015/mandated/150235.pdf)). How many Amharic interpreters are on the roster today could not be established; MDH's roster pages give no count by language.

Court interpreting is set by the Minnesota Judicial Branch. Its roster and certification pages would not open, so whether any court-certified Amharic interpreter works in Minnesota could not be confirmed.

**Teaching.** A 2023 Minnesota law created a free pathway for heritage language teachers to earn licenses. Sahan Journal reported in January 2025 that the first cohort of 47 teachers included Amharic and Tigrinya among its languages ([Sahan Journal, Jan. 6, 2025](https://sahanjournal.com/education/minnesota-teachers-heritage-language-licenses-hmong-karen-somali/)). The report does not say how many were Amharic teachers.

**Food, retail and services.** The grocery, restaurant and coffee trades are where Amharic is most heard in daily commerce (section 4). In 1999, the Merkato grocer's main business was teff flour and injera, sometimes more than 1,000 pieces on a weekend ([MPR News, 1999](https://archive.mpr.org/stories/1999/11/03/enuyes-merkato-ethiopian-grocery-store)).

**Many jobs at once.** The path of one Amharic-language publisher shows how work often stacks up. Sahan Journal reported in 2020 that after arriving in Minnesota, Henok Degfu worked at a Minneapolis bakery and then held nearly every housekeeping job at two hotels, up to director, while producing his English and Amharic newspaper at night and on weekends. He left hotel work at the end of 2017, when his outlet's advertising could support six full-time employees. The same story quoted Seble Asnake, owner of an adult foster care business in Columbia Heights, who had lived in Minnesota 34 years ([Sahan Journal, July 14, 2020](https://sahanjournal.com/profiles/ethiopian-journalist-zehabesha/)). Care work and small business both run through these accounts, but no Minnesota data show how common they are.

**Language as a workplace issue.** A Minnesota-specific study of Amharic speakers at work, or of unions with Amharic-speaking members, did not turn up.

findings: A roster without credential verification does not establish that Minnesota sets few rules for interpreting. Distinguish roster listing from qualifications and applicable setting-specific duties.
Narrow data-absence claims, remove unsupported most-heard commerce ranking and generalization from one publisher’s career.

source.heading: Religion and spiritual life
source.body:
Amharic is a language of worship for many Ethiopian Christians in Minnesota, and the churches are among the strongest Amharic-language institutions in the state. Ethiopian Minnesotans also include Catholic, Evangelical and Muslim communities, and some people of no faith; how many of them worship or gather in Amharic is not documented.

**Orthodox Tewahedo.** In the Ethiopian Orthodox church, the ancient language Ge'ez is used in the liturgy, alongside Amharic.

- **Debre Selam Medhanealem**, which opened a new church at 2601 30th Ave. S. in Seward in April 2026, holds Sunday services from 7 to 11 a.m. in Ge'ez and in Amharic, with some portions translated into English ([Longfellow Nokomis Messenger, April 27, 2026](https://www.longfellownokomismessenger.com/stories/debre-selam-medhanealem-ethiopian-orthodox-tewahedo-churchfinds-new-home-in-seward,161305)). Board Chair Debalke Gebeyehu called the church "a living bridge" for immigrants.
- **Worthington.** The congregation there, first established in 2010, has used the names Menbere Tsehay Sent Mary and Tsadakane Mariam in local coverage. In 2020 its project coordinator, Abebe Alubel, said members came from Ethiopia and Eritrea and spoke many languages, but nearly all spoke Amharic, so services were in Amharic. In 2022 the city council approved a permit for the church to move into The Globe's former office at 300 11th St. ([The Globe, 2020](https://www.dglobe.com/lifestyle/ethiopian-orthodox-church-almost-ready-to-build); [The Globe, March 29, 2022](https://www.dglobe.com/council-approves-new-home-for-ethiopian-church-oxford-street-reconstruction)). Whether the move was completed could not be confirmed.
- **Rochester.** St. George Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church was where a new store owner went to share his plans in 2024 ([Post Bulletin, 2024](https://www.postbulletin.com/business/rochester-welcomes-its-first-ethiopian-store)).
- The Ethiopian page describes Kidist Selassie Cathedral in Minneapolis and Debre Bisrat St. Gabriel and St. Arsema, whose new Rosemount building burned in July 2026.

**Evangelical.** The Ethiopian Evangelical Church in Minnesota, at 7360 33rd St. N. in Oakdale, lists a Sunday worship service in Amharic, a Wednesday service in Amharic, a Saturday young adult service in Amharic and a Sunday youth service in English ([EECMN](https://eecmn.org/)). That pattern, Amharic for adults and English for youth, shows in one schedule how a congregation is handling the generational shift. The Evangelical Mekane Yesus Lutheran Church Fellowship in Minnesota, 1566 W. Thomas Ave., St. Paul, reported average weekly attendance of 64 for 2025; its listing does not name a worship language ([Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod locator](https://locator.lcms.org/church/C/1001496)). Other Amharic-speaking Protestant congregations surely exist, but no other could be confirmed.

**Language classes in congregations.** Endalkachew Chala, a scholar and community member, wrote in June 2026 that there are roughly eight active Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox congregations in the metro, alongside Catholic, Evangelical and Muslim communities, and that each runs Amharic and Tigrinya classes for second-generation children ([MinnPost, June 2026](https://www.minnpost.com/community-voices/2026/06/celebrate-ethiopians-and-resilience-at-twin-cities-soccer-tourney-ethiopian-sport-federation/)). That is his description, and individual schedules were not checked.

**Where language divides worship.** In 2005, MPR News reported that two Minneapolis churches held services in Oromo, and that at one of them, Bethany Lutheran on Franklin Avenue, there were "unlikely" to be Ethiopians other than Oromo at the service. The reporter described a "loose self-segregation" rooted in the strife back home ([MPR News, May 19, 2005](https://archive.mpr.org/stories/2005/05/19/ethiopians-diverse-group)). That was 21 years ago and may have changed. It is a reminder that an Amharic-language service is a home for some Ethiopian Christians and not for others.

**Muslim Amharic speakers.** No Minnesota source described a mosque or Muslim association that worships or teaches in Amharic. The Ethiopian and Oromo pages discuss Ethiopian Muslim life more broadly.

**Fasting.** Grumdahl reported in 2024 that observant Tewahedo Christians over age 7 fast about 180 days a year, giving up meat and dairy ([Mpls.St.Paul Magazine, 2024](https://mspmag.com/eat-and-drink/the-new-ethiopian-scene/)). That affects meals at events, medicine taken "with food," and morning appointments.

One language schedule cannot establish individual or generational preferences. Do not guess additional congregations exist.
Fasting account must not become a rule for every person or medical instruction; ask the individual, and route medication advice to a qualified health professional.

source.heading: Celebrations and observances
source.body:
These are the observances most tied to Amharic-speaking church and community life. Dates and Minnesota events are in `calendar-entries.json`.

- **Enkutatash (Ethiopian New Year).** Falls on Sept. 11, 2026 and Sept. 12, 2027 ([Office Holidays, 2026](https://www.officeholidays.com/countries/ethiopia/2026); [2027](https://www.officeholidays.com/countries/ethiopia/2027)). The Ethiopian Community in Minnesota invited the public to a celebration at Highland Park Pavilion in St. Paul on Sunday, Sept. 13, 2026, from 2 to 7 p.m., with food, music, dance and traditional dress; the listing wrote the holiday's name in Amharic script ([Mefthe](https://mefthe.com/events/celebrate-ethiopian-new-year-in-minnesota/)). In 2022, the fourth annual Ethiopian Fest of Minnesota was held at Eden Prairie High School's stadium on Sept. 4, with concerts in West St. Paul, a fashion show and soccer; Henok Degfu said, "the Ethiopian New Year is coming" ([Eden Prairie Local News, Sept. 7, 2022](https://www.eplocalnews.org/2022/09/07/photo-gallery-ethiopian-fest-of-minnesota/)). A 2025 or 2026 Ethiopian Fest could not be confirmed.
- **Meskel (Finding of the True Cross).** Sept. 27, 2026 ([Office Holidays, 2026](https://www.officeholidays.com/countries/ethiopia/2026)). The Ethiopian page describes a Rochester bonfire celebration in 2022. No 2026 Minnesota Meskel event was found.
- **Genna (Christmas).** Jan. 7 in 2026 and 2027 ([Office Holidays](https://www.officeholidays.com/countries/ethiopia/2027)).

source.heading: Family, home and daily life
source.body:
**Households.** Compass counts about 12,436 Ethiopian-community households averaging 3.30 people. One-third are married couples with children, and 26.1 percent are people living alone ([Minnesota Compass](https://www.mncompass.org/topics/demographics/cultural-communities/ethiopian)).

**Language across generations.** The community is young: Compass counts 43.8 percent of the Ethiopian umbrella as 17 or younger ([Minnesota Compass](https://www.mncompass.org/topics/demographics/cultural-communities/ethiopian)), and those children are going through English-language schools. In one Oakdale church, adults worship in Amharic while young people have their own English service ([EECMN](https://eecmn.org/)). In 2005 an Oromo community member, Robson Itawa, put the worry plainly: the language will not die, he said, but for the second generation it will be mixed with English ([MPR News, 2005](https://archive.mpr.org/stories/2005/05/19/ethiopians-diverse-group)). His words were about Oromo, but Amharic-speaking parents face the same question. Weekend church classes, heritage language teachers and the state's bilingual seals (section 10) are the ways families and schools are answering it.

**Interpreting at home.** Whether children in Amharic-speaking homes end up interpreting for their parents, and how often, has not been studied in Minnesota as far as could be found. The current page's warning against using children as interpreters is sound practice in any language.

**Food.** Injera is daily bread. "Everybody at home has injera," Kebede Abay told the Post Bulletin, comparing it to bread for Americans ([Post Bulletin, 2024](https://www.postbulletin.com/business/rochester-welcomes-its-first-ethiopian-store)). Coffee ceremonies, with beans roasted and brewed in a clay jebena, are part of hospitality at home and at restaurants such as Selam ([From MPLS With Love](https://mplswithlove.com/guides/best-ethiopian-east-african-food)).

**Dress, marriage and aging.** Little was found that is specific to Amharic-speaking Minnesotans. Event invitations ask people to wear traditional dress ([Mefthe](https://mefthe.com/events/celebrate-ethiopian-new-year-in-minnesota/)). Only 3.5 percent of the Ethiopian umbrella is 65 or older ([Minnesota Compass](https://www.mncompass.org/topics/demographics/cultural-communities/ethiopian)), so the first large generation of Amharic-speaking elders is still ahead. The language needs of that generation in nursing homes, home care and memory care are a question to plan for, not yet a documented fact.

findings: Ethiopian-community household statistics are not estimates specifically for Amharic speakers.
A quoted Oromo-speaking family cannot establish what Amharic parents express; identify the question for inquiry.
Do not infer an Amharic elder-population forecast from the broader Ethiopian age profile. Attribute food description to the quoted retailer rather than declaring a universal practice.
